actions.justification: Mandatory first step - continuous vital sign monitoring is essential for any patient with acute dyspnea and chest pain to establish baseline and detect hemodynamic instability.

Mandatory - Wells score is the standard clinical decision tool for PE risk stratification in a patient presenting with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, especially in pregnancy which is a known risk factor for VTE.
Mandatory - D-dimer testing is part of the standard PE workup per guidelines. In conjunction with Wells score, it guides the need for further imaging (CTPA or V/Q scan).

A 12-lead ECG should be obtained within 10 minutes of first medical contact per AHA guidelines to evaluate for STEMI and other cardiac causes of acute chest pain. This patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, and ECG can also show signs of right heart strain consistent with PE (S1Q3T3 pattern, sinus tachycardia, right bundle branch block).

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain in pregnancy. An echocardiogram helps evaluate for right heart strain, which would support a diagnosis of pulmonary embolism — a critical concern in pregnancy. It also helps rule out other cardiac causes of dyspnea.

Chest X-ray is indicated to evaluate for alternative diagnoses and assess pulmonary vasculature in this pregnant patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. It is a low-radiation study appropriate as an initial imaging step before CT-PA consideration.

Supplemental oxygen should be administered to maintain adequate oxygenation, particularly important given the dual consideration of maternal and fetal well-being in this pregnant patient presenting with possible PE.

Pulmonology consultation is appropriate for this pregnant patient with suspected PE/acute dyspnea to assist with further workup planning (e.g., V/Q scan vs CT-PA) and management decisions given the complexity of anticoagulation and imaging in pregnancy.

ECG is essential for initial assessment of acute chest pain and dyspnea; the available action 'order_imaging_ecg' maps to obtaining a 12-lead ECG per AHA guidelines (within 10 minutes of presentation) to evaluate for arrhythmia or right heart strain pattern suggestive of PE in this pregnant patient.

This pregnant patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain has a high clinical suspicion for pulmonary embolism. After D-dimer and initial assessment, CT pulmonary angiography (or V/Q scan) is indicated to confirm or exclude PE diagnosis per PE management guidelines.

Echocardiogram is indicated to assess for right ventricular strain/dysfunction which would risk-stratify the patient and guide management decisions (e.g., need for thrombolysis) in suspected pulmonary embolism, especially given pregnancy complicates anticoagulation decisions.
ABG is indicated in suspected PE with dyspnea to assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status, which aids in risk stratification and management decisions.
BMP provides baseline renal function (important before contrast CT-PA if not yet run) and electrolytes, which are relevant for anticoagulation dosing and overall patient assessment.
Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound can identify DVT as the source of suspected PE and is safe in pregnancy, supporting diagnosis and guiding anticoagulation decisions.
CBC is indicated to evaluate for anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukocytosis in a pregnant patient with suspected PE, and helps guide anticoagulation decisions.
Coagulation studies (PT/aPTT) are needed prior to initiating anticoagulation therapy for suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy to establish baseline.
BNP helps assess right heart strain from potential pulmonary embolism, providing prognostic information alongside the CT-PA and echocardiogram already ordered.

Troponin is indicated to assess right heart strain from suspected PE in a pregnant patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Elevated troponin would indicate myocardial injury and help risk-stratify the patient per PE management guidelines.
Lactate level helps assess for tissue hypoperfusion and hemodynamic compromise, important for risk stratification of suspected PE even in a currently stable patient with normal vitals.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain in pregnancy — classic presentation for pulmonary embolism. Comprehensive diagnostic workup has been completed (CT-PA ordered, D-dimer, Wells score assessed). LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin) is the preferred anticoagulant in pregnancy for suspected/confirmed PE, as it does not cross the placenta and is safer than unfractionated heparin or warfarin. Initiating anticoagulation is indicated while awaiting CT-PA results given high clinical suspicion and stable hemodynamics.

Unfractionated heparin is appropriate anticoagulation for confirmed or high-suspicion PE in pregnancy, particularly as it can be rapidly reversed if delivery is imminent. Continuing anticoagulation after initial LMWH dose is guideline-concordant for PE management.

Supportive IV fluid administration may help maintain hemodynamic stability in the setting of PE, though patient is currently stable. Cautious fluid resuscitation is reasonable as a supportive measure.

Patient is pregnant with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, highly suspicious for pulmonary embolism. Anticoagulation (beyond initial heparin/LMWH already given) may need continuation or bridging. Given the clinical context of suspected PE in pregnancy, ongoing therapeutic anticoagulation is indicated per guidelines. This is the most appropriate available action given stable hemodynamics (vasopressors and thrombolysis not indicated; IR consult less urgent at this stage).

With suspected/confirmed PE in a pregnant patient who has already received anticoagulation, consulting interventional radiology is appropriate to evaluate for catheter-directed therapy options if the patient deteriorates or if CT-PA confirms massive PE, especially since systemic thrombolysis carries higher risk in pregnancy.
